Website builder, WordPress or custom development: what to choose

What to consider before development: content management, platform limits, integrations and ongoing costs. A comparison based on RESET projects.

A website builder is useful when its ready-made tools meet the requirements and help launch quickly. WordPress is worth considering when a team regularly manages content and wants to develop the project on a widely used CMS. Custom development makes sense for specific user journeys, data handling or integrations that are difficult to implement on the chosen platform.

The choice affects everyday work: who changes a property's price, adds a page, fixes a form and pays for services. Compare ongoing costs alongside development. An inexpensive first version may be costly to expand, while a complex content management system may be unnecessary for a site updated only a few times a year.

01

Website builders, WordPress and custom development: the differences

A builder provides a visual editor and ready-made infrastructure. WordPress is a content management system extended through themes, plugins and custom code. With custom development, the team chooses the architecture, libraries and data management approach to match the project.

The approaches overlap. A builder can include a CMS, WordPress can use a custom theme, and a bespoke interface can connect to an existing CMS. Here, WordPress means the WordPress.org software installed on your chosen hosting. WordPress.com has its own hosting terms and plans.

What to compare before choosing a platform
CriterionBuilderWordPressCustom development
LaunchFast with a suitable template and prepared contentDepends on the theme, modules and modificationsDepends on features and available components
EditingThrough the editor and available CMSThrough a configured administration panelThrough a connected CMS or a developer
CatalogueWithin platform and plan limitsUsing configured content types and modulesBased on an agreed property and search model
IntegrationsAvailable connectors, APIs and service limitsPlugins, APIs and custom modificationsCustom logic within external API constraints
Ongoing costsSubscription, additional services and site workHosting, any licences and maintenanceInfrastructure, external services, support and development

Site format is a separate decision. Landing pages and multi-page websites can use different technologies. If the format is still undecided, start with Landing page or multi-page website: choosing for advertising and SEO.

02

When a builder helps

At RESET, we primarily consider builders for clear requirements and tight deadlines: a campaign page, a service presentation or a test of an offer. A suitable template and prepared text and images can reduce the work.

Tilda, Webflow, Framer and Wix fall into this category. Their capabilities differ, so the editor's appearance is not enough to choose between them. Content management, integrations, catalogue limits and hosting terms matter.

A builder can also suit a team without a permanent developer. Staff can learn the editor, update content and publish within prepared templates. Such a site may serve a business for years; whether it is temporary depends on the plan, not the platform label.

RESET receives fewer builder requests than custom development tasks. This reflects our projects, rather than a claim that builders have become irrelevant to the wider market.

03

Why a builder is not always cheaper

A ready-made template and a custom design require different amounts of work. Creating an original layout, adapting it to mobile screens, configuring a catalogue and routing enquiries still require effort regardless of the editor.

For example, assembling standard Tilda blocks and creating an individual page in Zero Block can involve very different workloads. Both still require structure, copy, images, form behaviour and final checks.

RESET estimates that a builder project with a CMS may need around $800-1000 or more, depending on requirements. This is a guide to website creation work. Platform subscriptions, paid add-ons, content preparation and subsequent changes should be budgeted separately.

Compare equivalent scopes: page types, languages, content, integrations and testing. A low assembly price does not tell you the cost of a complete, usable product.

04

Hosting and migration: what to check before paying

Visual platforms have different export terms. Downloading files does not necessarily mean that the CMS, forms and search will work on another server.

  • Framer includes publishing and hosting. Its documentation states that HTML export for self-hosting is unavailable.
  • Wix hosts sites on its own infrastructure. Its architecture does not support moving a working site to external hosting.
  • Webflow supports code export on an appropriate plan, but does not export the whole platform. CMS features, form processing and other functions need separate arrangements outside Webflow. See the export documentation.
  • Tilda supports export on an appropriate plan. Check hosting and feature requirements in the platform instructions before moving.

Plans and conditions can change. Establish recurring charges, account ownership, content export and migration requirements before starting. Discuss the domain, data and editor access alongside design.

05

When to choose WordPress

WordPress suits teams that regularly publish and update services, articles, case studies or property listings. It can also support a small site; choosing WordPress says little about company size.

Its strength is an established content management foundation that can be extended. The official features overview covers publishing, user management and extensibility.

For property websites, useful fields should be designed for price, area, location, status and photographs. Staff need to understand where to edit information and how it appears. An administration panel alone does not ensure a convenient workflow.

In RESET's experience, WordPress projects often continue growing on the same platform with new sections, design updates and modules. If the foundation meets the requirements, replacing the technology may be unnecessary.

Maintenance remains necessary: update the system, themes and plugins, keep backups and check key journeys after changes. The WordPress maintenance guide also covers these tasks. More dependencies require more careful compatibility management.

06

When custom development is worth the investment

A custom approach makes sense when the business needs logic that is awkward to assemble from available modules. An agency may need a unified property database, complex matching, synchronisation between sources or integration with its own CRM.

Custom systems also use existing libraries and components. The team chooses the tools and takes responsibility for their combined behaviour, security and maintenance.

AI can help with repetitive tasks and speed up testing ideas. RESET uses it as a working tool. It does not remove the need to design data structures, verify integrations or take responsibility for the result.

Estate CRM for DELMAR illustrates business-specific logic: enquiries are connected to the property database and client selections. The technology serves employees' daily actions.

Development freedom brings obligations. Establish who maintains the code, how hosting works, where backups live and whether another team can take over. A bespoke system without documentation or a clear handover also creates supplier dependence.

07

Who will update prices, listings and text?

Ask this before development. Without a CMS, content changes usually go through a developer. That may be acceptable for occasional edits, but inconvenient for a daily catalogue update.

A custom website can use a CMS. Editors do not need control over everything. Often it is enough to manage properties, services, prices, news, staff and contacts, while the development team controls the layout and structure.

After developing a custom-coded site, RESET provides one month of support for agreed content changes, such as information and price updates. We define the scope when agreeing the project. New functionality and substantial structural changes are quoted separately.

For frequent updates, we recommend planning a CMS. The aim is to let clients handle recurring content tasks independently. Technical maintenance and feature development remain separate.

08

Which is better for SEO and advertising?

Assess the actual implementation. A builder site can have the required SEO controls, while a bespoke one may contain technical errors. Tilda, for example, explains its SEO features in its guide.

For property sites, we check whether the required pages can be created, URLs and metadata controlled, technical duplicates excluded and sections connected with internal links. Catalogues also need workable filters, crawlable property pages and updated data.

Speed depends on images, scripts, third-party widgets, servers and content loading. A platform name cannot replace testing on mobile devices.

For advertising, we check the match with the ad, clarity of the offer, working forms and event tracking. If a builder meets these requirements, using it does not inherently weaken advertising. Limits matter when a necessary journey cannot be implemented or developed reliably.

See our articles on real estate SEO for structure and Google Ads for the relationship between ads and landing pages.

09

Comparing launch costs and ownership costs

Budget for a complete period, such as the first year. Include the domain, hosting, licences, maintenance and expected changes alongside development.

First-year budget

Development + content preparation + domain and hosting + subscriptions and licences + technical support + planned changes.

A builder may include some infrastructure in its subscription. WordPress costs are divided between hosting, add-ons and specialist work. Custom infrastructure depends on the architecture; a connected CMS may also have a paid plan.

A limited support package might be discussed at around $100-200 per month. This is an illustrative budget requiring a defined task list and limits. Regular catalogue uploads, new modules and emergency recovery involve different workloads.

For example, hypothetical support at $150 per month totals $1800 a year. This excludes other costs and is not a RESET tariff. It illustrates why support terms should be discussed before commissioning a site.

We break development estimates into clear components so clients can compare a launch without a CMS with one that includes independent editing. See project cost examples in our article on building websites with AI.

10

When to change platforms

RESET has moved projects from Tilda to custom development because of growth constraints and search requirements. Each decision addressed specific limitations in structure, data management or functionality.

Low search visibility alone does not justify a move. Content, missing pages, indexing errors or a weak offer may be responsible. First identify a constraint that the new technology would actually resolve.

There is no universal progression from builder to WordPress to bespoke system. One project stays on WordPress and gains modules. Another starts with a custom interface and adds a CMS later. A third remains on a builder while it meets the requirements.

During migration, we preserve useful content, map old URLs to new ones, configure redirects and check forms, analytics and integrations. For SEO migration, we follow Google's guidance on URL changes. A move does not guarantee traffic growth, and recrawling takes time.

11

How RESET chooses a solution

We begin with business objectives and team workflows: the offers being promoted, visitor sources, enquiry handling and responsibility for content.

  1. 01

    Define essential journeys

    List pages, properties, forms, languages and user actions. Record advertising and SEO requirements separately.

  2. 02

    Check data and integrations

    Identify catalogue sources, update frequency, CRM connections and responsibility for accuracy.

  3. 03

    Compare scope and costs

    Assess launch, maintenance and near-term changes. Check platform constraints before design begins.

  4. 04

    Agree on management and handover

    Define what clients can edit, which accounts and permissions they receive, and how the site will develop after launch.

A ready-made platform is suitable if it meets the needs with clear costs. When the editor or modules impose limits, we consider custom development. The choice should be explainable through specific features, budget and team workflows.

12

Questions before choosing a platform

Can a builder website rank in Google?

Yes. Check the platform and implementation: page structure, content accessibility, metadata and technical settings. The platform alone guarantees no rankings.

Is WordPress only for large websites?

No. It can support small projects too. What matters is whether content management and maintenance fit your workflow.

Can I edit a custom site without a programmer?

Yes, with a connected and configured CMS. Decide which data editors can access during planning.

Is a website without a subscription free to maintain?

No. Domain, server, external services, support and modification costs can remain even without a builder subscription.
